title: Indian Fort Mountain
summary: In Madison County, Indian Fort Mountain is a Woodland hilltop enclosure ringed by low walls of stone and earth that once led people to imagine a fort.
bodyMarkdown:
Indian Fort Mountain is a wooded knob in Madison County. Archaeologists record it as site 15Ma25. Its summit is ringed by low walls of stone and earth, and for many years the name led people to imagine a fort and a battle. Current research tells a different story.

## A hilltop enclosure

The [Kentucky Heritage Council's survey of the Woodland period](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Learn-More/Documents/Woodland%20Period%20Chapter%20The%20Archaeology%20of%20Kentucky%20An%20update%20Volume1.pdf) describes Indian Fort Mountain as a hilltop enclosure. Its irregular stone-and-earth walls stand 1 to 2 meters high and enclose about 25 hectares. The site is part of a cluster of Woodland sites in the Knobs of Madison County.

## Dating the walls

Writers including Young (1910), Burroughs (1926) and Tincher (1973) speculated about the earthwork's purpose. The first excavation the Heritage Council cites is by the archaeologist Moore, reported in 1982, who dug a small trench across a section of the wall. He recorded how the wall was built but found no diagnostic artifacts, the kind of tools or pottery that can be tied to a particular culture.

Two radiocarbon dates came from the work. Moore rejected the older one, which pointed to about 580 B.C., and accepted a calibrated date of 39 B.C. to A.D. 236.

That date places the site in the Late Adena timeframe, according to the Heritage Council. The same chapter adds a caution. The site "may not be related to Adena," because hilltop enclosures in southern Ohio are usually associated with the [Hopewell tradition](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hopewell_tradition). The National Register of Historic Places record, as summarized by [AsNotedIn](https://www.asnotedin.com/?action=travel&id=L0043840), lists the site's cultural affiliation as Hopewell and its period as Middle Woodland, 200 B.C. to A.D. 500.

## Not a fort

Early surveyors saw the stone walls and wrongly concluded that the mountain was the site of a battle and a fort. The [Kentucky Heritage Council's survey of the Woodland period](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Learn-More/Documents/Woodland%20Period%20Chapter%20The%20Archaeology%20of%20Kentucky%20An%20update%20Volume1.pdf) describes a hilltop enclosure, not a stockade.

## Respecting the site

Visitors who find chert flakes, broken points or pieces of stone tools should leave them in place. Removing artifacts strips them of their context and of what they can teach.

## Kentucky today

The mountain is a popular hiking area in Madison County, and the trails cross ground with a long Native history. Other Woodland earthworks in Kentucky include [Mount Horeb](/stories/mount-horeb-earthworks/) and the [Old Fort Earthworks](/stories/old-fort-earthworks-15gp1-greenup-county/) in Greenup County.
